extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, fundamental properties, and key theorems about dimension and codimension in algebraic geometry (for schemes and finitely generated k-algebras), including Krull dimension, Noether normalization, dimension = transcendence degree, codimension behavior, and related lemmas/theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: dimension of a topological space (Krull dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dimension of a topological space X (denoted dim X) is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible sets, starting the indexing of the closed irreducible sets with 0. (The dimension may be infinite.) Scholars of the empty set can take the dimension of the empty set to be −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is purely topological and does not use the structure sheaf. Analogy: the dimension of a vector space is the supremum of lengths of chains of subspaces. For rings, dimension is defined as supremum of lengths of chains of nested prime ideals (indexing starts at 0); this is often called Krull dimension. Use examples and exercises (e.g., Show dim Spec A = dim A) to translate between the topological and algebraic viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: dimension of a ring and relation dim Spec A = dim A
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the dimension of a ring as the supremum of the lengths of chains of nested prime ideals (indexing starts at zero). Show that dim Spec A = dim A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 3.7.E (bijection between irreducible closed subsets of Spec A and prime ideals of A) and the homeomorphism Spec A ≅ Spec A/N(A) to relate nilpotents. This algebraic formulation is the standard Krull-dimension notion for affine schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention: dimension of the empty set
rubrics_metrics.description: The dimension of the empty set may be taken to be −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a convenient convention for theorems and exercises; treat the empty scheme consistently with this convention in proofs and inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: equidimensional / pure dimensional
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space is equidimensional or pure dimensional if each of its irreducible components has the same dimension. If each irreducible component has dimension n we say it is equidimensional (or pure dimensional) of dimension n. An equidimensional dimension 1 (resp. 2, n) space is said to be a curve (resp. surface, n-fold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dimension behaves oddly for disjoint unions, it is often preferable to talk about irreducible or pure-dimensional spaces. Many theorems (e.g., codimension = dimension difference) assume purity or irreducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-cover characterization of dimension (Exercise 11.1.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme has dimension n iff it admits an open cover by affine open subsets of dimension at most n, where equality is achieved for some affine open subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical method of checking the dimension of a scheme by reducing to affine pieces; the exercise gives a hint about bijection between irreducible closed subsets of U and those of X that meet U.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples of dimension (11.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identified prime ideals of k[t] (0 and (f(t)) for irreducible f), Z ((0) and (p)), k (only (0)), and k[x]/(x^2) (only (x)). Hence dim A1_k = 1, dim Spec Z = 1, dim Spec k = 0, dim Spec k[x]/(x^2) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as sanity checks for the definitions. Compute primes and chains of primes to determine dimensions of common rings/schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-local behavior of dimension: dim(Z)=max(dim X,dim Y) for unions
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z is the union of two closed subsets X and Y, then dim Z = max(dim X, dim Y). Thus dimension is not a 'local' characteristic of a space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when reasoning locally vs. globally; prefer talking about dimension of irreducible spaces when possible. This motivates definitions like equidimensionality and statements restricting to irreducible/variety hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian scheme of dimension 0 has finite number of points (Exercise 11.1.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a Noetherian scheme of dimension 0 has a finite number of points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an 'easy exercise' illustrating finiteness properties of Noetherian schemes of low dimension (use in pathologies/counterexamples consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers of integral morphisms have dimension 0 (Exercise 11.1.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is an integral morphism, then every (nonempty) fiber of π has dimension 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to Y = Spec k and show that for an integral extension φ:k→A, dim A = 0 by showing every nonzero element is invertible in an integral domain finite over a field. Use base-change preservation of integrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension preserved under integral extensions (Exercise 11.1.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:Spec A → Spec B corresponds to an integral extension of rings, then dim Spec A = dim Spec B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove that a chain of primes downstairs gives a chain upstairs of the same length using Going-Up Theorem; conversely, use Exercise 11.1.D to show no two elements of the chain upstairs map to the same downstairs element. This is important when passing between finite/integral extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and dimension (Exercise 11.1.F & 11.1.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ν:X'→X is the normalization in a finite extension of fields, then dim X'=dim X (allowing integral/affine hypotheses for convenience). If X is an affine k-scheme and K/k an algebraic field extension, then pure dimension is preserved under base change (X_K has same pure dimension n as X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises show dimension behaves well under normalization and algebraic field extension; hints reduce to affine/integral domain cases and use Noether normalization/Exercise 11.1.E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: codimension of an irreducible closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible closed subset Y ⊂ X, define codim_X Y as the supremum of lengths of increasing chains of irreducible closed subsets starting with Y (indexing starts at 0). The codimension of a point is the codimension of its closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the naive formula dim X − dim Y except in safe contexts; codimension defined this way is robust even when dim X = ∞. Use this definition when reasoning about local behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Height/codimension of a prime ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime ideal p in a ring has codimension equal to the supremum of lengths of chains of decreasing prime ideals starting at p (indexing at 0). This is often called height; codim of p in A equals dim A_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate between geometric codimension and algebraic height via Spec. Use standard facts (e.g., in integral domain the ideal (0) has codimension 0). See §3.2.8 for the relation dim A_p = codim p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality codim_X Y + dim Y ≤ dim X (11.1.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is an irreducible closed subset of a scheme X, then codim_X Y + dim Y ≤ dim X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inequality can be strict in general; warning and figure illustrate pathologies. For irreducible varieties (finite type over a field) equality holds (Theorem 11.2.9). Use counterexamples (later in the book) to understand failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: codimension-1 primes in a UFD are principal (Lemma 11.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a unique factorization domain A, all codimension 1 prime ideals are principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: choose a nonzero f∈p, pick an irreducible factor g∈p, then (g) is a nonzero prime ideal contained in p; since p has codimension 1, conclude p=(g). Note the converse holds under Noetherian hypotheses (see Proposition 11.3.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathology: existence of infinite-dimensional Noetherian rings (Exercise 11.1.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nagata's construction shows a Noetherian ring of infinite Krull dimension exists: start with A=k[x1,x2,...], choose an increasing sequence of integers m_i with increasing differences, define certain prime ideals and localize to produce S^{-1}A which is Noetherian but has infinite dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This counterexample warns that Noetherian does not imply finite dimension without locality; exercises give steps to construct and verify properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: dimension = transcendence degree for finitely generated domains (Theorem 11.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely generated domain over a field k, then dim Spec A = tr. deg K(A)/k. Hence for an irreducible k-variety X, dim X = tr. deg K(X)/k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This powerful interpretation links algebraic/transcendence notions to geometric dimension. Theorem is proved via Noether normalization and induction (see 11.2.7). Consequences: dimension of An_k is n; dimension can be computed on any nonempty open set of an irreducible finite-type k-variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noether Normalization Lemma (11.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an integral domain, finitely generated over a field k, and tr. deg_k K(A) = n, then there exist algebraically independent x1,...,xn ∈ A such that A is a finite (hence integral) extension of k[x1,...,xn]. Geometrically: any integral finite-type affine k-scheme X admits a surjective finite morphism X→A^n_k where n = tr. deg K(X)/k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nagata's proof is given: write A=k[y1,...,ym]/p and reduce the number of generators by non-linear 'jiggling' z_i = y_i - y_m^{r_i} with carefully chosen exponents r_i so that ym becomes integral over the subring. Geometric intuition: project generically to a hyperplane to obtain a finite morphism; for infinite base fields, linear choices suffice; for finite fields Nagata's nonlinear trick is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of affine space An_k equals n (part of 11.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: dim A^n_k = n. Demonstration: produce an explicit chain of irreducible closed subsets of length n using coordinate hyperplanes, and argue upper bound via induction using irreducible hypersurfaces and induction on transcendence degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact is used repeatedly as a base case in inductive arguments; check chains of prime ideals in k[x1,...,xn] and use irreducible polynomials to reduce dimension by 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a dominant rational map (11.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X --→ Y is a dominant rational map of irreducible k-varieties of the same dimension, the degree of the map is defined as the degree of the corresponding field extension K(X)/K(Y). For reducible X, sum degrees over components; if not dominant, degree is 0. Degree is multiplicative under composition: deg(ρ∘π)=deg(ρ)deg(π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic definition corresponds geometrically to counting preimages of a general point of Y (see 24.5.10). Use for mapping degree computations and composition properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension is the difference of dimensions for irreducible varieties (Theorem 11.2.9 / 11.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X a pure-dimensional k-scheme locally of finite type and Y an irreducible closed subset with generic point η, dim Y + dim O_{X,η} = dim X. Hence for irreducible varieties (finite type over a field) codim_X Y + dim Y = dim X; inequality (11.1.4.1) is an equality in this setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to showing that a maximal proper closed irreducible subset Z of an irreducible affine k-variety X has dim Z = dim X − 1, using Noether normalization and the Going-Down theorem. This is a key structural property for varieties (finite type over a field).

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Down Theorem for finite extensions of integrally closed domains (Theorem 11.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose φ:B→A is a finite extension of rings, B is an integrally closed domain, and A is an integral domain. Given nested prime ideals q⊂q' of B and a prime p' of A lying over q', there exists a prime p of A contained in p' that lies over q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analog of the Going-Up Theorem for the reverse inclusion direction under integrally closed hypotheses. The proof uses passing to integral closure in a normal closure of the field extension and applying Galois automorphisms (see Lemma 11.2.15 and prime avoidance). Geometric intuition: extend chains of primes downwards in finite maps when base is integrally closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime avoidance (Proposition 11.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p1,...,pn are prime ideals of a ring A, and I is an ideal not contained in any pi, then I is not contained in the union ∪ pi: there exists f∈I not in any pi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful technical lemma in many algebraic arguments (e.g., in the proof of Lemma 11.2.15). Geometric interpretation: one can find a function vanishing on none of a finite collection of irreducible closed subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity of Galois automorphisms on primes of integral closure (Lemma 11.2.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let B be an integrally closed domain, L/K(B) a finite normal field extension, and C the integral closure of B in L. If q' is a prime ideal of B, then Aut(L/K(B)) acts transitively on the prime ideals of C lying over q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the proof of Going-Down: conjugate prime ideals via automorphisms to move primes and then descend to A. The proof uses prime avoidance and properties of norms (or product of conjugates) to reach a contradiction if transitivity fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remarks on preservation of dimension under arbitrary field extension (Exercises 11.2.J and 11.2.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a locally finite type k-scheme of pure dimension n and K/k is any field extension, then X_K has pure dimension n (Exercise 11.2.J) — this needs finite type hypotheses. Without finite type hypotheses the statement can fail (counterexample noted in 11.2.16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 11.2.J suggests writing K/k as algebraic over a purely transcendental extension and reducing to known cases; use for verifying dimensional invariance when extending scalars for finite-type schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preview: Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem and Algebraic Hartogs's Lemma (Section 11.3 introduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Krull’s Principal Ideal Theorem generalizes the linear algebra fact that a single linear equation cuts out a subspace of codimension 0 or 1; algebraic Hartogs’s lemma links functions and the codimension one points where they vanish. These results will require (locally) Noetherian hypotheses and are technically harder, but crucial for computing codimensions and characterizing UFDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect Krull’s Principal Ideal Theorem to give bounds on heights of primes containing principal ideals (e.g., height ≤ 1 in appropriate contexts) and Algebraic Hartogs to provide extension/uniqueness results for functions across codimension ≥2 subsets. The chapter advises focusing on how to use these theorems rather than memorizing proofs.
